label: Symplectic Manifolds
notes: This chapter, printed pages ninety-four through one fifty-one, lifts the linear symplectic form onto a manifold. The carrier is a closed nondegenerate two-form. We will track exactly what Darboux and Moser preserve, and why the geometry has no local invariants at all beyond dimension.

label: Definition of a Symplectic Manifold
notes: A symplectic manifold pairs an even-dimensional smooth manifold with a two-form that is simultaneously closed and nondegenerate. Closedness is a differential equation on the form, while nondegeneracy is a pointwise determinant condition. Together they force orientability and supply a canonical volume form built from omega.

label: Closed and Nondegenerate
notes: Nondegeneracy means the form induces an isomorphism between tangent vectors and covectors at every point. Closedness, the vanishing exterior derivative, is the integrability condition that makes Hamiltonian flows preserve omega. Drop either property and the rich rigidity theory of later chapters simply collapses.

label: The Standard Model R^2n
notes: Euclidean space carries the constant Darboux form, a sum of wedge products of conjugate coordinate pairs. This standard model is the reference every other example is measured against. Its matrix is the block J, and nondegeneracy reduces to J being invertible everywhere on the space.

label: Cotangent Bundles
notes: Every cotangent bundle is symplectic through the tautological one-form, whose negative exterior derivative gives the canonical two-form. This construction is coordinate-free and governs classical phase space. The base manifold sits inside as a Lagrangian zero section, while fibers are themselves Lagrangian subspaces of the bundle.

label: More Examples
notes: Oriented surfaces are symplectic by their area form, since any nowhere-zero two-form on a surface is automatically closed. Complex projective space carries the Fubini-Study form, and Kahler manifolds supply a vast family where the symplectic and complex structures are compatible through a Riemannian metric.

label: Darboux's Theorem
notes: Darboux's theorem is the structural heart of the chapter: near any point a symplectic form looks exactly like the standard model in suitable coordinates. Consequently symplectic geometry has no local invariants beyond the dimension. All interesting questions are therefore global, motivating the rigidity results that follow.

label: The Moser Argument
notes: Moser's trick proves Darboux and many isotopy results uniformly. One interpolates between two cohomologous forms and solves for a time-dependent vector field whose flow pulls one form back onto the other. The key algebraic step inverts nondegeneracy to define that vector field from a primitive.

label: Moser Stability
notes: On a closed manifold, a smooth family of cohomologous symplectic forms is connected by ambient diffeomorphisms. The cohomology class is the only obstruction to deforming one form into another. This stability statement is what upgrades the pointwise Darboux normal form into a genuine global flexibility principle.

label: Submanifolds by Restriction
notes: Submanifolds are classified by how omega restricts to their tangent spaces. Symplectic submanifolds keep nondegeneracy, isotropic ones kill the form, and coisotropic ones contain their own symplectic orthogonal. Lagrangians are the maximal isotropic case, sitting at exactly half the ambient dimension and central to everything later.

label: Weinstein's Neighborhood Theorem
notes: Weinstein's theorem says a Lagrangian submanifold has a neighborhood symplectomorphic to a neighborhood of the zero section in its own cotangent bundle. Thus the embedding carries no local invariants either; only the diffeomorphism type of the Lagrangian and its normal data matter for the local model.

label: Contact Structures
notes: Contact structures are the odd-dimensional companions of symplectic geometry. A contact form satisfies a maximal nondegeneracy condition: alpha wedged with the top power of its exterior derivative never vanishes. Such forms arise naturally as boundary data and on hypersurfaces of contact type inside symplectic manifolds.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We defined symplectic manifolds, surveyed their examples, and proved that Darboux and Moser remove all local invariants. Submanifolds were organized by restriction, Weinstein localized Lagrangians, and contact geometry entered as the odd-dimensional cousin. The remaining chapters chase the global rigidity these normal forms make visible.
